title: The Best Way to Teach Soft Skills
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership argues that social skills such as empathy, listening, advocacy and conflict resolution cannot be taught by rules the way technical skills can, which is why workshops and discussion groups so often fail. The recommended alternative is the practice clinic, where team members try out choices across varied scenarios and get immediate feedback. Through trial and error they build a repertoire, learn which tactics work, and gain confidence to try new behaviors. The post adds that leading organizations now supplement clinics with AI and virtual reality role-play available on demand. Its conclusion is blunt: situational practice and heavy repetition are the only reliable route to social competence.
points: Soft skills resist rule-based teaching, which explains why conventional training programs rarely move the needle.
Practice clinics built on realistic scenarios and immediate feedback are presented as the effective method.
Reflecting on which tactics work or fail helps people see how much how they speak and act matters.
AI and virtual reality role-play are described as useful on-demand supplements to live clinics.
quotes: The so-called soft or social skills — such as empathy, listening, advocacy, and conflict resolution — are difficult to teach and nearly impossible to scale across an organization. Despite their role in creating high-performing and effective organizations, social skills have proven elusive to develop in team members and leaders. That’s because most organizations go about teaching them in the wrong way.

To learn social skills, team members must practice their choices in a variety of situations, scenarios, and critical episodes. Through trial and error with immediate feedback, team members build a repertoire of effective approaches and strategies. The more practice they get, the better they become.

Practice clinics that expose peers to situations that reflect the complexity and nuances of real-time challenges work best to build skill. Focusing on what approaches might work best and what tactics would likely underperform teaches team members how to appreciate what they say and do, and how they say and do it tremendously influences their ability to succeed.

Many of the best contemporary organizations supplement their practice clinics with AI and virtual reality practice sessions that team members can access at any time. The ability to role-play and work through an unlimited set of situations at their own pace further enhances the skill development that begins in such clinics.
Teaching social skills requires situational practice and a heavy dose of repetition. Nothing else works very well. As it turns out, practice is the best instructor.
